prime.problem: A data agent's golden case stores an expected answer, but the warehouse keeps changing under it. Without more than a stored number, a healthy agent fails the test after a backfill, a wrong query passes because it happens to match, and you can't tell whether the agent or the data moved.
prime.fits: You know how to run tasks with repeats and intervals, and how to order graders (deterministic first, judge last). This card applies both to an agent whose ground truth is a live warehouse, the last piece of the data-agent course after receipts.
expect: the data boundary (snapshot, as-of, current reference query, invariants)
a judge sharing the agent's blind spot
prime.goal: Given a golden case on live data, pick the comparison strategy, say what it can and can't catch, and design a release gate that wouldn't hide a broken slice or a changed grader.

attend: Why does the fixed golden value fail the healthy agent in October but pass the deprecated-table agent?
What does rerunning on the July snapshot tell you, given that it passes all three agents?
Why does a path check catch in July what every result-only grader misses?
How can the overall score rise from 79.5% to 81.0% while Finance drops to zero?
Why does a grader change need its own frozen human-labelled set rather than the agent's golden cases?

must: The warehouse changes legitimately (late refunds, backfills, metric revisions) → a fixed expected value goes stale → it fails the healthy agent and can pass a stale path that froze at the same moment → every case needs a recorded data boundary or a current reference query

A wrong path can return today's right number (deprecated table, missing filter, bad join) → result-only grading passes it → also check the path: required and prohibited tables, filters, metric version, invariants

A model judge reasons from the same definitions as the agent → it rewards a fluent answer built on a shared wrong definition → put metric contracts, reference execution and invariants ahead of the judge, and calibrate it against human labels
The overall score is a case-weighted mean of slices → a small slice can collapse while the average rises → set thresholds per critical slice and make policy and critical-metric failures hard blockers
elevated: A snapshot rerun is a classifier, not a correctness check → it separates "agent changed" from "data changed" but passes bugs that only show on new data (the missing intercompany filter) → pair it with canaries and replay on live data

The grader is an answer-changing artifact → changing tolerance from exact to ±1% moves October from 1/3 to 2/3 right verdicts with no agent change → version graders and test them on a frozen human-labelled set
reference: the full golden-case field list (question, canonical intent, metric contract, sources, tables, reference SQL, data boundary, expected result, policy result, evidence, ambiguity policy, slice tags)

the release path in order: change manifest → component evals → critical end-to-end suite → repeated trials → baseline and slice comparison → review → shadow or canary → rollout → monitoring → promote or roll back
the list of comparison strategies (exact scalar, normalized tables, subset/superset, tolerance, invariants, current reference query, SQL semantic analysis, human review)
the OpenAI Evals API dates (read-only 2026-10-31, shutdown 2026-11-30)

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the July and October columns for the three EMEA agents and say, for each grading strategy, why it gets the verdicts it gets. Then write 3–4 sentences on what a golden case on live data must contain beyond an expected number.
checklist: July: all three agents return the same number, so only a path check separates them
October: the fixed value fails the healthy agent and passes the stale table, because both froze in July
the snapshot rerun tells you who moved (agent or data) but can't catch bugs that need new data
a current reference query or invariants decide correctness on live data; a path check catches the wrong evidence
release gates per slice, and the grader versioned and tested like any other artifact

retrieve.q: Explain why "the agent's answer changed" can't be called a regression unless the case records a data boundary, and name three kinds of boundary.
answer: the change could come from the agent or from legitimate data change (late arrivals, backfill, metric revision, schema migration, freshness incident)
a boundary lets you rerun on the old data or compute today's right answer
kinds: fixture, versioned snapshot, time-travel id, as-of timestamp, current reference query, invariants

retrieve.q: Walk through the October run of the legacy-table agent under the fixed golden value, the current reference query and the path check. What does each grader read and decide?
answer: fixed golden: reads 46.30, compares to 46.30 stored in July → PASS (wrong verdict)
current reference query: runs canonical SQL today → 46.05 ≠ 46.30 → FAIL (right)
path check: reads the table from the receipt/SQL → deprecated table → FAIL (right)

retrieve.q: A teammate proposes widening the tolerance so late refunds stop breaking the suite. What does that buy and what does it cost?
answer: buys: the healthy agent passes small legitimate drift (±1% passes 46.05)
costs: it still passes the stale table, and a wider band (±3%) passes the missing-filter agent too
it is also a grader change, so it should be versioned and checked against human labels

retrieve.q: When is a model judge the right grader for a data-agent case, and when must it be overruled?
answer: right for: whether claims are supported, assumptions visible, ambiguity handled
never overrides a policy failure, a broken invariant or a clear result mismatch
it can share the agent's wrong definition, so calibrate it against human labels and track disagreement

compare.q: The Tuesday run's grader reads a test exit code; the EMEA case's grader reads a number from a warehouse. What makes the second harder to ground, and how does the grader-ordering rule carry over?
answer: a test's pass/fail is stable on fixed code; a warehouse number legitimately changes over time
so the data agent's ground truth needs a boundary or a current reference query, not a stored value
same rule: deterministic checks (policy, structure, results, invariants) before any judge, and the judge never overrides them
both fail the same way when the judge sees only what the agent saw or shares its definitions

compare.q: Measuring an agent fought noise from random trials. This card fights a different source of error. Which, and would more trials or more tasks fix it?
answer: the error here is in the expected value and the slice weighting, not in sampling
more trials don't help: a stale golden value fails the healthy agent every time
more tasks help only if they cover the broken slice; otherwise the average still hides it
you need both: intervals for noise, boundaries and slice gates for drift

predict.q: The metric owners revise "net revenue" to subtract a new chargeback provision, and update the canonical reference query, but the agent's context still describes the old definition. Which strategies from the table now flag the agent, which of those verdicts are right, and what should happen to the golden case?
predict.answer: The current reference query flags it, correctly: the agent is answering the old definition. The fixed golden value and the snapshot rerun don't notice, because they encode the old meaning. The path check flags it only if it checks the metric version. Per the post, a semantic-definition change should bump the metric version and update the affected cases explicitly, because the new number is the intended result; the agent's context then needs the same versioned change.

apply.task: Copy code/changing-data-evals.py, change TOL from 0.01 to 0.03 and rerun. Before you run it, predict the October row for the tolerance strategy. Then add one invariant strategy of your own that catches the missing intercompany filter without knowing the golden value.
apply.done: Your ±3% run prints P P P right 1/3 for October (47.45 is +2.48%, inside 3%), and your invariant strategy marks the no-IC agent F in October.
apply.hint: An invariant can compare the answer with the canonical sales − refunds for the same rows: any extra amount means something the contract excludes got in.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the ±3% row, or which strategy notices a metric revision?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the snapshot rerun passes everyone, or why it's still worth having?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: data change → stale golden value, or stale golden value → passing a stale path?
In a data agent you've seen, which slice would an average most likely hide?
Which grader in your own evals has changed without anyone versioning it?
